The đàn tỳ bà (Vietnamese pipa) is a traditional Vietnamese plucked instrument and a chordophone, descended from the Chinese pipa. Its body is wooden and pear-shaped and carries four nylon strings, silk strings early on; it is held almost vertically and played with a small plectrum, larger than a guitar pick, while the left hand stops the strings and bends or plucks them frequently to make inflected sounds. Two forms exist: the traditional pipa, held at a slant, and the reworked pipa, held vertically with four frets replaced by high position marks, which is the common one today. The instrument was once associated with court occasions and is still used in performances of the court music of the Huế palace.

初學可先採近垂直角度持琴，現今越南琵琶多為直抱形式。右手以較吉他撥片稍大的小型撥: A beginner can start by holding the instrument almost vertically, since the Vietnamese pipa is mostly played that way today. The right hand plucks the four strings with a small plectrum, a little larger than a guitar pick; the left hand stops the strings and frequently bends or plucks them with the fingers to produce different sounds. For tuning, start with the common C f g c and then practise stopping the strings and bending.

琵琶的琴身採用梨形設計，面板通常以杉木製作，背板則使用楓木或其他硬木。琴頸多為紅: The body of the pipa is pear-shaped, the top usually of spruce and the back of maple or another hardwood. The neck is mostly of mahogany, strong and good acoustically. The tuning pegs are of wood or ivory. The four strings were traditionally of silk; modern pipas also use nylon or steel strings. The frets are of hardwood, and the crescent-shaped plectrum is carved from tortoiseshell, ivory or plastic.
琵琶音色明亮穿透，具有金屬般的光澤感，兼具溫潤的質感。其音域寬廣，從低音的沉厚渾: The pipa's timbre is bright and penetrating, with a metallic sheen and warmth as well. Its range is broad, from a deep, murky low register to a crisp, sharp high one, spanning more than three octaves. It resonates in its own way: the pear-shaped resonator and the four strings act together to produce rich overtones and harmony. The timbre changes constantly in playing, the tremolo technique making a continuous stream of sound while rapid plucking gives a crispness like pearls dropping onto jade. Beside the guqin the pipa is brighter and stronger; beside the guitar it keeps more of an Eastern softness. Its characteristic onomatopoeic effects, such as “ai” and “beng”, give it great expressive power in traditional music.

越南琵琶（Đàn tỳ bà）屬弦鳴樂器，源自中國琵琶，先於中國流行，再傳入東亞: The Vietnamese pipa (đàn tỳ bà) is a chordophone descended from the Chinese pipa; it was popular in China before spreading to East Asia, and reached Vietnam around the Trần dynasty. Its name is a Vietnamese rendering of the Chinese “pipa”. In the Lý and Trần dynasties, and possibly into the Later Lê, its form was close to the Japanese biwa and it is no longer used today. From the Nguyễn dynasty on, influenced by the Ming and Qing pipa and adjusted to Vietnamese musical culture, it was long used on court occasions and is still found in the court music of the Huế palace.
